author: By John Malamatinas, Contributor
title: TikTok Revolt in France: A New Generation Takes To The Streets
content:
On October 17, France witnessed some of the most intense urban unrest in its recent history. Hundreds of thousands of people demonstrated across the country, while clashes with police, widespread looting, and burning barricades transformed the streets of numerous cities. Activists described the events to Unicorn Riot as among “the fiercest riots France has experienced since World War II.”




The protests were not confined to Paris. From Marseille and Lyon to Bordeaux, Limoges, and numerous smaller cities, demonstrators confronted police, occupied streets, and attacked commercial and government buildings.










The mobilization had begun weeks earlier. On September 7, a young TikToker called for a revival of the Yellow Vests movement, which had shaken France in 2018 and 2019. The immediate trigger of the original movement was the rising price of fuel, which had climbed above two euros per liter.




Meanwhile, an independent wave of high school protests was spreading across France. Students were protesting deteriorating school infrastructure, chronic underfunding of public education, and worsening conditions in classrooms. Hundreds of schools were reportedly occupied or blockaded during the preceding weeks.




These two mobilizations began to reinforce each other, turning October 17 into a focal point for broader social discontent. On TikTok, a veritable media storm unfold

author: By Sean Summers, Unicorn Riot
title: Line 5 Opponents Confront Wis. Gov. Evers: ‘Drink the Future Water of Lake Superior’
content:
Milwaukee, WI — As Governor Tony Evers took the stage during the annual Wisconsin Association for Justice dinner, an audience member rose to lead a toast for the state’s leader.




But rather than honoring Evers’ accomplishments, the patron issued a challenge. Thrusting a glass of thick black fluid into the air, Tom Hoy asked Evers to drink the liquid which served as a representation of Lake Superior’s waters which protesters say will be contaminated by oil and other hazardous waste from Enbridge’s Line 5 pipeline if the state, and Evers specifically, doesn’t revoke the company’s construction permits.
















“I have a glass of water with crude oil,” Hoy announced, holding aloft a cup filled with liquid resembling oil-laden water. “Will you drink the future waters of Lake Superior, sir?”




Hoy, an activist with the group 

Climate Defiance

, continued to challenge Evers to have a drink as attendees, security personnel and police shoved them out of the audience and toward the door.




Protesters attended the dinner calling on Evers to reject the pipeline not on vague objections to the project but under specific conditions spelled out in the state’s agreement with the company.

author: By L. Cam Anderson, Contributor
title: How The Proud Boys Lost Their Name
content:
West Palm Beach, FL – On Sept. 26, the film “American Martyrs” premiered at the Kravis Center’s Cohen Pavilion in West Palm Beach, Florida. 




The subject of the film, presented by the far-right media outlet Gateway Pundit, was the Proud Boys – specifically the “seditious five,” whom a federal jury found guilty of seditious conspiracy to stop the presidential transfer of power for their role in the Jan. 6, 2021 storming of the U.S. Capitol.







The official poster for the film, promoted by Enrique Tarrio and Gateway Pundit on X ahead of its premiere. Note that Zachary Rehl, first on the left in the lineup, is AI-generated.







The five Proud Boys presenting the film were chairman Henry “Enrique” Tarrio, Ethan Nordean, Joe Biggs, Zachary Rehl and Dominic Pezzola. In reality, the actual fifth member of the “seditious five” is Jeremy Bertino, not Pezzola, who pleaded guilty and testified against the others during their trial. 




In August 2025, Bertino appeared on an episode of Tarrio’s Substack podcast titled “Kiss of Judas,” where the “government star witness” allowed the permanently sunglasses-clad chairman to humiliate him for the twelve people who liked the post. Despite this entreaty to re-enter the flock, Bertino did not make the cut as an “American martyr.”

author: By Darren Thompson, Contributor
title: Mining in the Sacred and Stolen Black Hills, Then and Now
content:
The colonization of the Black Hills by the U.S. government is one of the most well-known land thefts in American history. Since gold was discovered in the sacred lands of Paha Sapa or Ȟe Sápa, also known as the Black Hills, more than 150 years of tragedy, land exploitation, and legal issues followed and continue to this day.




When rumors began to spread in the 19th century that gold was found in the Black Hills, U.S. Army General George Armstrong Custer led a 1,000 man expedition in 1874 to find out for himself. When the discovery became public, thousands rushed to the Black Hills — trespassing on Indian Territory — to also find out for themselves.




The Black Hills were then a part of the Great Sioux Reservation and belonged to the Great Sioux Nation as promised in the Fort Laramie Treaty of 1868 which reserved lands for the exclusive use and occupation by the Great Sioux Nation, including the Black Hills. Any cession of any part of the reservation required a new treaty executed and signed by at least three-fourths of all adult male Indians occupying the land. 




One of the provisions of the 1868 Treaty was that white men were forbidden from stepping foot on the reservation, except for officials of the U.S. government.

author: By Elvis Takahashi Mantello, Contributor
title: Marco Rubio’s Visit to Athens Raises Questions About Western Democracy
content:
Athens, Greece – U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio visited Athens to talk about democracy and to deepen political ties with the right-wing Greek government. However, his visit also stirred public outcry, with demonstrators showing anxiety about Greece’s growing militarization and the potential to get entangled in foreign conflicts.




Rubio arrived last Tuesday evening for the sixth round of the U.S.-Greece Strategic Dialogue. By the next day, he stood on Pnyx Hill, the Acropolis behind him, and delivered a speech that invoked ancient Greece to defend Trump’s “America First” approach. He called on Europeans to “awaken from their long slumber.” His nationalist speech called for dominance in supply chains and future technologies. 

CNN

 and the 

Washington Post

 viewed the speech as a campaign ad for his potential candidacy in the 2028 U.S. elections.




Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis described Greek-U.S. relations as being “

at the highest level ever

,” while Rubio referred to Greece as “such a strong partner.” The leaders announced that Greece agreed to spend up to 

$4 billion on a U.S. arms deal

 along with a joint counterterrorism program.




Yet, the streets of Greece during Rubio’s visit told a different story.

author: By L. Cam Anderson, Contributor
title: Jake Lang’s Tour of American Courtrooms Continues
content:
St. Paul, MN – White supremacist agitator and violent J6er Edward Jacob “Jake” Lang Zoomed into a court hearing in St. Paul on Friday, Oct. 9, as the Minnesota state government argued its case against him for kicking over an ice sculpture reading “Prosecute ICE” in front of the State Capitol building in February.




The hearing marked Lang’s second appearance for his 

criminal charges

 after the previous hearing scheduled for July was canceled. It saw the state’s attorneys make the case for a hate crime charge in addition to property destruction against Lang that could carry a prison sentence, while Lang’s attorney argued in favor of a pretrial hearing to dismiss the additional charge.




Lang, wearing a polka dot dress shirt beneath a navy blue suit jacket, was making his video call from a familiar location where he frequently gives interviews, sitting in front of a backdrop branded for his “Blessed News Network,” which markets itself as “AI-curated Christian and conservative headlines.”







Jake Lang appearing on a monitor hanging above the court room.

 

Photo contributed by L. Cam Anderson.







The previous day, Lang was protesting at Cornell University in New York, carrying a sign on campus claiming the “Cornell 7” were innocent, potentially explaining his absence in the Minnesota court room. According to Lang, he was “thrown out” of the campus for this.

author: By Camilla Donzelli, Contributor
title: Greek Trials Turn Migrants Into ‘Smugglers’ and Minors Into Adults
content:
Crete, Greece — Crete’s courts are convicting shipwrecked people on the move as “smugglers” in trials lasting minutes, with lawyers documenting minors registered as adults and sentences reaching hundreds of years.




Eleftheria Iatraki lets her gaze wander along the walls of the room as she tells the story of Thalassa of Solidarity. The shelves are crowded with books, sewing machines, toys, and other objects. “We created this place as a space to meet each other through learning activities — sewing classes, language classes, computer classes,” she explains. She wears a black T-shirt reading “no one is illegal,” her elbows resting on the table that fills the small room where the collective carries out its activities.







Eleftheria Iatraki speaks with Unicorn Riot in the space where Thalassa of Solidarity holds its activities. Photo contributed by Romanos Lioutas.







Through the glass door facing the street, the white facades of the buildings in central Heraklion, Crete’s regional capital, are visible.

author: By Hannah Kass and Ryan Fatica, Contributors
title: Historic Trees Demolished, Land Defenders Arrested and New Treesit at US-Mexico Border
content:
Lochiel, AZ – In the early hours of October 5, Border Patrol agents raided the anti-border camp called “Tierra Libre” on the U.S.-Mexico Border near Lochiel, Arizona. An estimated 200 Border Patrol Agents invaded camp — entering the tracts of private property along the border that had long-shielded land defenders from the authority of the federal agents — and cut down the ancient Grandmother tree that campers had attempted to protect. Less than 24 hours later, land defenders established a new treesit in the immediate path of construction, this time on the Mexican side of the border. 




Although Border Patrol agents were parked along the easement throughout the night, a masked land defender snuck past them and scrambled up into the 50-foot-tall Grandmother tree and into the platform already built there. “This brave warrior climbed right up there,” said Pablo, a land defender who was at camp Tuesday morning. “The new treesit is very much blocking construction, as long as someone is in that tree they will not be able to build their wall.”

author: By Brendan Maslauskas Dunn, Contributor
title: Waging Peace in a Time of War in Thailand and Cambodia
content:
The fog of war has not fully dissipated from the mountains and dense forests of Cambodia and Thailand’s borderlands, well over a year after the two nations became ensnared in deadly clashes. It is still unclear who fired the first shot, although both governments blame the other side for starting the conflict. Both armies left a wake of destruction in many of the normally peaceful, serene villages and towns along the border. It may take years to repair the damage caused by the fighting. 




At the peak of the conflict, 

rockets rained down on houses and hospitals in Thailand

. Civilians at a 7-Eleven in Thailand met their fate in an inferno of flames 

caused by a Cambodian rocket that struck the building

. In Cambodia, children ran in a panic when their schools were evacuated. Thai F-16 fighter jets flew over Cambodia on 

bombing missions

.




The ancient Khmer (Cambodian) temple and UNESCO World Heritage site 

Preah Vihear was barraged by ordnance from the Thai army

, 

shattering parts of it into pieces

.

. Hundreds of thousands of Thai and Khmer civilians were displaced from their villages, and moved into makeshift shelters. Many have not yet returned home.

, with many more wounded. The Royal Thai Army laid to rest 43 soldiers. The Cambodian government has not publicly disclosed the

author: By Elvis Takahashi Mantello, Contributor
title: Nikos Romanos Acquitted As Greek Government Pushes Terrorism Cases
content:
Athens, Greece — Testing Greece’s controversial terrorism law, Greek anarchist Nikos Romanos, alongside Argyrios K. and Dimitris P., was acquitted of terrorism charges earlier this year in connection with an explosion in an apartment in Athens in October 2024.




For the same case, Marianna Manoura was sentenced to 19 years in prison on explosives and terrorism charges, while Dimitra Zarafeta received an eight-year sentence.




The charges against Romanos were centered on a partial fingerprint found on a plastic bag where the accidental explosion occurred in the Ampelokipi neighborhood. The investigation turned into a terrorism case and renewed attention on Romanos who previously gained notoriety in 2008 after witnessing the 

police kill his friend Alexandros Grigoropoulos

, which triggered weeks of unrest across Greece.







A mural of Alexandros Grigoropoulos in Exarcheia, Athens, at the corner of Messologiou and Tzavella streets, near the site where he was shot. Photo contributed by Elvis Takahashi Mantello.







Greece’s Terrorism Law & A Partial Fingerprint

author: By Niko Georgiades, Unicorn Riot
title: Israel Bombs Newly Built Water Desalination Plant in Gaza
content:
Gaza, Palestine — For nearly two months, Palestinians in Gaza City’s Sheikh Radwan neighborhood had access to water at any time — a welcome sense of stability in the depths of a genocidal war. On Aug. 24, that stability was disrupted by an Israeli airstrike that destroyed the newly built water desalination plant and damaged apartment buildings and tents.




Standing next to rubble and forcibly displaced from the airstrikes, Louay Al-Namnam told Unicorn Riot that at least 14 Palestinian families were now looking for “somewhere to live.”




“We were sitting safely inside the complex,” he said, “when suddenly someone approached us and told us to leave because the area was about to be bombed. A water desalination plant was struck first, and then the complex itself was hit.”



















“We are all now out on the streets. We need somewhere to live! We couldn’t salvage any of our personal belongings—we escaped with nothing but the clothes on our backs, just as you see us now. What kind of truce is this? What kind of humanity allows this to happen to us?”




Louay Al-Namnam, forcibly displaced by Israeli airstrikes in Gaza City













The water plant had provided free desalinated water to families and over a dozen shelters and collectives. The bombing worsens Gaza City’s drinking-water crisis which impacts 92% of the population.

author: By Dingane Xaba, Unicorn Riot
title: South African Graffiti Artists Reflect on Past Present and Future
content:
Durban, South Africa — “In the early days we were painting on two-by-one Masonite boards,” said Iain Robertson, a Durban-based graffiti artist who goes by the name 

Ewok

. “That’s how we would do exhibitions as graffiti artists … we’d built our own walls. And this meant that we had to work within quite tight parameters.” 




For many years, this was the environment South African graffiti artists had to work under, much of this owing to the generally negative attitudes surrounding graffiti art since its inception in the 1960s. Fast forward to 2026 and societal perceptions around graffiti art have drastically shifted as high-profile art studios and even billion dollar companies have steadily embraced the art form.
















South African Graffiti Artist Unveils Anti-Consumerist Mural in Durban




Long gone are the days when graffiti artists were largely viewed as parasites and blights to society. To the contrary, many of those same once ostracized artists have now become revered as cultural icons. Any one living in a major city merely need step outside their door to see the evidence for themselves. 




There is no urban environment in the world where graffiti has not made it’s mark. Even in places like Durban — an area mostly known for being the birthplace of Shaka Zulu — there exists a thriving and unique graffiti art community.




History of Graffiti Art and Spread
